entry.title: Canonical Quantization on Cotangent Bundles
entry.content:
Canonical Quantization on Cotangent Bundles

In typical physics textbooks, canonical quantization transfers a Hamiltonian MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_0@@ defined on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_1@@ by replacing MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_2@@ with MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_3@@ and MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_4@@ with the multiplication operator MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_5@@, yielding a densely-defined operator on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_6@@. This works perfectly for Euclidean space in Cartesian coordinates. However, the simple replacement framework does not work in general coordinates.

A simple example: the kinetic energy of a particle of mass MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_7@@ in spherical coordinates MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_8@@ is

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_9@@

The naive replacement MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_10@@ gives

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_11@@

while the correct kinetic energy operator (the one used for, e.g., the hydrogen atom) is the Laplace-Beltrami operator

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_12@@

Their difference is the first-order operator

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_13@@

So MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_14@@ and the simple replacement fails. This note develops the correct, coordinate-free definition of canonical quantization for Hamiltonians that are fiberwise polynomial of degree at most 2 on a cotangent bundle.

Setup

Let MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_15@@ be a smooth manifold with a volume form MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_16@@, let MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_17@@ be the Hilbert space of complex square-integrable functions on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_18@@, and let MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_19@@ be its cotangent bundle. A quantization is a linear map from a subspace of real functions on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_20@@ to a subspace of densely-defined self-adjoint operators on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_21@@.

We define canonical quantization for:

  • MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_22@@ — the space of fiberwise-polynomial functions of degree MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_23@@ on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_24@@,
  • MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_25@@ — the space of self-adjoint differential operators on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_26@@ of order at most 2.

The non-triviality is that the simple replacement

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_27@@

is not coordinate-independent — it is not a well-defined intrinsic operation.

Decomposition by Fiber Degree

The space MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_28@@ has a canonical direct sum structure

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_29@@

where each summand consists of functions homogeneous of degree MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_30@@ in the fiber variable MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_31@@. For any MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_32@@, the decomposition MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_33@@ is given intrinsically (without coordinates) by:

  1. MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_34@@
  2. MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_35@@
  3. MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_36@@

This decomposition uses only the vector space structure of the fibers MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_37@@, not any metric or connection. We then quantize each piece separately.

Zeroth Order

The space MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_38@@ consists of fiberwise-constant functions, which are essentially smooth functions MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_39@@ pulled back along the fiber projection MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_40@@. The quantization is simply the pointwise multiplication operator

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_41@@

First Order

A fiberwise-linear function on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_42@@ is a smooth section of MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_43@@ — that is, a vector field MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_44@@. In local canonical coordinates MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_45@@, the function MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_46@@ corresponds to the vector field MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_47@@ on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_48@@.

The naive quantization MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_49@@ is not self-adjoint. A direct computation shows that the MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_50@@-adjoint of MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_51@@ is

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_52@@

where MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_53@@ is the divergence of MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_54@@ with respect to MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_55@@, defined as the unique smooth function satisfying

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_56@@

or equivalently MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_57@@ via Cartan’s formula. In local coordinates with MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_58@@, this is MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_59@@.

The resolution is to take the self-adjoint part:

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_60@@

This is the unique formally self-adjoint first-order differential operator with principal symbol MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_61@@, given the volume form MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_62@@.

Second Order

A fiberwise-quadratic function MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_63@@ corresponds canonically to a symmetric contravariant 2-tensor MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_64@@ via the polarization identity: MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_65@@. In local coordinates, MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_66@@ corresponds to MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_67@@.

The symmetric 2-tensor MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_68@@ determines a second-order operator up to a first-order term — different choices of affine connection give different second-order operators with the same principal symbol, differing by first-order operators. The key result is that the self-adjointness requirement pins down a unique choice:

Theorem. For any MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_69@@, there is a unique element in the corresponding family of second-order differential operators that is self-adjoint as an operator on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_70@@.

Proof (uniqueness). Suppose MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_71@@ and MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_72@@ are both self-adjoint and have the same principal symbol, so MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_73@@ is a self-adjoint first-order differential operator. The adjoint of MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_74@@ on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_75@@ is MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_76@@. Self-adjointness MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_77@@ forces MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_78@@, hence MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_79@@ and MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_80@@.

Proof (existence). The operator

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_81@@

is self-adjoint on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_82@@. Indeed, for compactly supported MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_83@@:

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_84@@

The coordinate-free description is MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_85@@, where MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_86@@ contracts one index of MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_87@@ against MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_88@@ to produce a vector field, and MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_89@@ is then applied. When MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_90@@ and MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_91@@, this recovers the Laplace-Beltrami operator MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_92@@.

Higher Orders

Unfortunately, the story stops here. For fiberwise-cubic (and higher) functions, the analogous correspondence still exists — a fiberwise-degree-MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_93@@ function determines a family of order-MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_94@@ operators sharing the same leading symbol, differing by order-MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_95@@ operators. However, the uniqueness theorem fails for MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_96@@.

In the third-order case, two self-adjoint operators in the same family can differ by a self-adjoint first-order operator MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_97@@, and the only constraint from self-adjointness is that MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_98@@ is divergence-free with respect to MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_99@@. The space of such vector fields is infinite-dimensional, so the ambiguity is genuine. This is consistent with the Groenewold-Van Hove obstruction, which asserts that no quantization map on polynomials of degree MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_100@@ can simultaneously satisfy the Poisson bracket relation, act irreducibly, and extend the Schrödinger representation.

Summary

We constructed a canonical quantization on the cotangent bundle of a smooth manifold MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_101@@ equipped with a volume form MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_102@@, mapping fiberwise polynomials of order at most 2 on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_103@@ to densely-defined self-adjoint operators on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_104@@. The procedure is:

  1. Decompose MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_105@@ into homogeneous parts: MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_106@@.
  2. Quantize each part by formulas (zeroth order), (first order with symmetrization), and (second order via divergence form).
  3. Sum: MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_107@@.

In local canonical coordinates MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_108@@, the quantization of MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_109@@ is

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_110@@

where MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_111@@ are scalar functions of MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_112@@ and MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_113@@. This differs from the naive replacement by the first-order correction

MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_114@@

which vanishes in Cartesian coordinates on MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_115@@ (where MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_116@@ and MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_117@@) but is nonzero in general curvilinear coordinates.

In a Hamiltonian system from classical mechanics, a Riemannian metric MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_118@@ determines the kinetic energy and the natural volume form MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_119@@. In this case the kinetic energy operator quantizes to MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_120@@, and for a particle of mass MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_121@@ in three-dimensional Euclidean space (MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_122@@) this becomes the familiar MATH_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER_123@@.

entry.title: Welcome to the Research Blog
entry.content:
Welcome to my new research blog! This space will feature short articles on computational mathematics, machine learning for PDEs, stochastic methods, and scientific computing.

What to Expect

In this blog, I’ll be sharing:

  1. Research insights from my work on deep learning methods for PDEs
  2. Tutorial-style articles on scientific computing techniques
  3. Updates on recent developments in computational mathematics
  4. Thoughts on the intersection of mathematics and machine learning

How This Blog Works

This blog system is designed to be simple and flexible:

  • Articles are written in Markdown format
  • Each article includes metadata (title, date, author, tags)
  • The system automatically parses and displays articles
  • You can write new articles by creating Markdown files

Example Code

Here’s a simple Python example of a numerical method:

import numpy as np

def finite_difference(f, x, h=1e-5):
    """Compute finite difference approximation of derivative."""
    return (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h)

# Example usage
def example_function(x):
    return x**2 + np.sin(x)

x_value = 1.0
derivative = finite_difference(example_function, x_value)
print(f"Derivative at x={x_value}: {derivative}")

Looking Ahead

I’m excited to share more content on topics like:

  • DeepMartNet for solving elliptic PDEs
  • Weak adversarial training for Fokker-Planck equations
  • Stochastic computing methods
  • Geometric approaches to machine learning

Stay tuned for more articles, and feel free to reach out with questions or suggestions!

Andrew Qing He
